From Arabic via Italian and Spanish, with letter-salad spellings. A [[boomerang word]]: Levantine Arabic borrowed it back as ardishawki, folk-etymologized as 'earthy thorny'.

Built up through Johnny Appleseed, early American cookbooks, pie as a symbol of prosperity, and WWII soldiers fighting for 'mom and apple pie'.
A variant of [[arse]] through the same sound loss that gives [[cuss]] from [[curse]].

To make a fool of someone; a [[be-]] word that still comes up a little today.

From French for lion's tooth, after the jagged leaves; also called blowballs, clocks, [[piss-a-bed]], [[cankerwort]], milk witch and Irish daisy.
A yellow-orange Crayola colour retired in 2017 to make room for Bluetiful, inspired by YInMn Blue; it became a collector's item and returned in 2025.
Called a Shakespeare coinage, clipped from the earlier [[dawning]], perhaps to fit his pentameter; also mentioned in the Shakespeare episode.
From a Proto-Germanic root meaning to burn or be hot, likely from a heat-related Proto-Indo-European root. It is related to a Sanskrit word for a glow in the sky.
A 13th-century word for dawn; Jess says it reminds her of the video game Skyrim.
A British political term for a shocking distraction, as if a dead cat were put on the table so no one discusses the real issue.
Means having nothing going on, being bored or wasting time; the source of the band name [[Die Toten Hosen]].
The name for a ten-day week in the French Revolutionary calendar, where each 30-day month had three; it meant ten days, not ten years.
A French technique name that literally just means 'cutouts'.
First meant any beast or animal and later narrowed to the specific animal, as seen in [[wilderness]].
In Old English it meant any wild quadruped, not only a deer; it survives in the middle of [[wilderness]].
Originally Deaf Leopard, coined in a school art lesson and respelled for fun; the band liked that it echoed [[Led Zeppelin]].
From Latin lira, 'furrow'; the verb meant to go off the furrow, the classical equivalent of [[off the rails]].
A place without people, not a sandy place; from Latin deserere, to unjoin or forsake, which is related to [[series]].
Comes from a different Latin root than [[dessert]], one meaning to join together or put in a row; a deserted place is cut off from humanity.
An island that is deserted, not a sandy island as Rob had long assumed; see [[desert]].
The course eaten after the table is 'disserved', or cleared of everything else; unrelated to [[desert]], but shares the verb 'serve' with [[just deserts]].
To stray away from the course, from [[via]].
Being devious or deviant means straying from the moral path, from [[via]].
Originally 'lasting one day', from [[dies]]; a doublet of [[journal]], covered in a previous episode.
German band whose name means the doctors.
German band whose name comes from the idiom [[dead trousers]], meaning to have nothing going on.
Its meaning is unknown and it's probably part of a longer phrase; theories include gratitude, 'barely fills your stomach' and 'so close to the heart'.
Latin prefix meaning not, away or broadly, as in distribute; French words beginning de- or des- carry the same prefix after it passed through French.
From medieval Latin dies mali, the two unlucky days each month, also called [[Egyptian days]]; first used in 'in the dismal', then the tautological 'dismal day'.
From medieval Latin dies mali, two unlucky days a month on calendars. It entered English as 'in the dismal', making 'dismal day' a tautology.
Literally not knowing which way east is, from [[orient]]; Rob says it means 'to un-east yourself' and finds Americans prefer it.
The British form; per Rob it means undoing an orientation you had, a tiny difference from [[disorient]]; it's built on [[orientate]].
From an Old English word for deer, alongside the source of [[hart]].
Rob's 'dog mystery': its origin is unknown, other languages only borrow it, and its -og ending recurs in [[frog]], [[hog]], [[stag]] and [[pig]].
Origin unknown; one of a puzzling set with [[frog]], [[hog]], [[pig]] and [[stag]] that had an Old English double G, probably starting as cutesy diminutives that replaced [[hound]].
Cockney rhyming slang for the telephone, given as an example of rhyming slang in everyday British speech.
Old English lacked a general [[shark]] word, using specific names like houndfish or sea dogs, which survive as dogfish.
A French word for certain dog breeds, borrowed from English [[dog]].
Borrowed from English [[dog]], like similar words in other languages; it usually means a mastiff, probably because Britain's best-known exported dog was the [[mastiff]].
From Greek delphis, womb, probably because they give birth to live young, though possibly because of their shape.
William the Conqueror's compendious volume charting who owned what land, brought up in connection with [[doom]].

term: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko
original: Nikkō o mizu shite kekkō to iu nakare
translation: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko

mentions.note: Praises Nikko's shrine complex and puns on 'Nikko' and 'kekko' (splendid); the hosts compare it to Goethe's [[see Naples and die]].

term: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge
translation: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge

mentions.note: Advice to stay out of other people's business and problems.
Old English dom meant a law, decree or judgment, extended to a decision determining fate or destiny; it is also the -dom in [[kingdom]].
An old word for a judge, from [[doom]] in its sense of judgment; Jess thinks it a great name.
From Latin dorsum, the back, which is a handy way to remember where the dorsal fin is.
Thought to mean 'dry', from a Germanic seafaring phrase for dry goods or barrels. It covered spices, herbs and medicines, then narrowed to apothecary wares.
Cotton duck, or duck canvas, is a tightly woven kind of canvas; this sense of duck comes from Dutch.
Began as non-adhesive strips of [[duck]] cloth called duck tape; the name moved to adhesive tape in WWII, and 'duct tape' is a folk etymology.
Began as a non-adhesive strip of [[cotton duck]] cloth named after the fabric. The name later passed to the plastic-coated adhesive tape WWII soldiers used.
Johnson defined it as 'not exhilarating, not delightful', with the self-referential example 'to make dictionaries is dull work'.
The same word as dusky, meaning the darkest part of the day that isn't night; Old English dox underwent metathesis, like [[ask]] and axe.
Meant ground, like Latin terra, before it referred to the planet.
From the Dutch word for donkey, a thing that carries loads, much like a clothes horse; so an easel holding a canvas is a donkey carrying cannabis.
Borrowed from Dutch ezel, 'donkey'; Jess compares it to the animals in [[clothes horse]] and [[sawhorse]].
From a root meaning to become light, where the sun rises; related to Sanskrit ushas 'dawn', [[aurora]] and [[australis]]; unusual beside Germanic ost-forms.
Greek echidna meant snake or viper, so it is unclear why a hedgehog-like animal got the name; the link to [[echinoderm]] is uncertain.
Sea cucumbers' group; the name can mean spiky skin or hedgehog skin, linked to Greek echinos, hedgehog, and possibly [[echidna]].
The Old English word, with cognates including Latin anguilla, meaning little snake or serpent.
A Middle English word, used into the 19th century, meaning 'soon afterwards'; Jess suggests reviving it.
Freud, writing in German, called it das Ich, 'the I', rather than the Latin ego.
Another name for the dies mali behind [[dismal]], supposedly calculated by ancient Egyptian scholars or linked to the story of the plagues.
German for squirrel, which Rob thinks involves folk etymology; like Dutch and other Germanic words for squirrel, it relates to the oak, as does [[acweorna]].
Now has an almost solely crude meaning, but originally just meant to exclaim.
The painter was called 'the Greek' because he was a foreigner where he worked; he grew up in Venetian-ruled Crete and worked in Italy and Spain.
Not actually a true [[eel]], but a member of a completely different order.
The hosts struggle with elk versus [[moose]]: they are different animals, but moose are called elk in some parts of the world.
One of the words Jess used with fifth graders to teach a Latin root meaning 'to talk', along with [[loquacious]] and [[soliloquy]].
Used in southwest England as an insult for people not from the area, especially tourists.
From Greek empatheia, 'passion, inner feeling'. It's a [[false friend]] of Modern Greek empatheia, which means animosity or malevolence.
Painting with pigment in heated beeswax, used in ancient Greece, Egypt and Rome; it is the 'grandparent' of the modern [[crayon]].
A fairly transparent lost word meaning the day of one's death.
Its Greek root means cut into, like [[insect]] in Latin; confusing it with [[etymology]] inspires a joke Jess hears almost daily.
A starter in British English but the main dish in North America. Wartime and Depression-era restaurants repositioned entrées as filling enough to replace the main course.
Someone sent somewhere to represent someone else; from [[via]] and related to [[invoice]].
The Old English name for April, 'Easter month'.
The top ocean zone; the pelagic element means of the sea or of the open sea.
Named because it divides the earth into equal parts, the hemispheres.
Literally equal night, one of the transparent calendar terms along with [[solstice]].
German suffix showing where something comes from, found at the end of [[frankfurter]], [[wiener]] and [[hamburger]].
A lost English word for the day before yesterday; compare German [[vorgestern]]. The hosts want to revive it with [[overmorrow]].
Belching; Rob recalls a dictionary, possibly Johnson's, describing it as a gassy, meaty-smelling emission.
French for east, borrowed from English [[east]], like the other French compass points, and then into Spanish.
From Dutch etsen, 'to cause to be eaten', so it is related to [[eat]]: etching eats away at a surface. It is unrelated to [[sketch]].
A Louisiana dish, usually made with crawfish, with sauce poured over it; the name just means smothered in French.
A reassuring saying that even experts sometimes make mistakes.
A reaction to [[Impressionism]], which it saw as too focused on outward experience; it expressed inner experience through distorted forms and exaggerated colours.
Descends from the same fork-shaped ancient letter as [[U]], [[V]], [[W]] and [[Y]], with the fork leaned over.
Means the thing opposite or facing you, which is why a clock or watch has a face that looks at us.
The American name for the season, with a sense of decaying and dying; like [[autumn]], it replaced the older [[harvest]], and is unusual among Germanic languages.
A word that looks like a word in another language but means something different, like [[empathy]] and its Modern Greek lookalike.
From a French word meaning 'to stuff'. Farces were comic relief rammed in to pad out serious productions, for example during set changes.
Bow-tie pasta, whose Italian name means butterflies.
In Quebec French, like 'fasten your seat belt'; a toque here is a winter hat, though the word can also mean a chef's hat.
Roman calendar lists of official and religious events and of dies fasti, days allowed for business; Jess enjoys that the source is 'the fasti of Furius'.
A Scottish word in the hosts' list of regional rain words; Jess thinks it generally means gross.
From Middle English 'fisting [[cur]]' (farting dog); it first described lively little dogs, supposedly because ladies blamed their farts on their lapdogs.
From felis, the classical Latin word for cat, which is older than the Late Latin cattus behind [[cat]].
A common cat name meaning happy or lucky, popular thanks to Felix the Cat and its likeness to Latin felis, source of [[feline]].
Another Old English word for a marsh.
Ultimately from a word meaning 'robber', as in Italian; English took it from French furet, which Rob links to fuir 'to flee'.
Originally meant sending your hunting [[ferret]] after something, not acting like a ferret; ferrets were domesticated to chase rabbits out of warrens.
A fan praised their music as fettes Brot, slang for really good hash, since fett meant great and Brot meant hash.
A classic dog name meaning faithful or trustworthy, related to [[fidelity]].
The classic dog name comes from Latin fidus, 'faithful', and is related to [[fidelity]]. In the 1940s a famous Italian dog named Fido waited daily at a bus stop.
A sassafras powder that the Choctaw contributed to [[gumbo]] as a thickener; the French term is related to [[filament]], meaning ropy or turned into threads.
A joke in the Philippines that Filipino time means being late; many cultures joke similarly, for example about [[Indian Standard Time]].
An old word for a midwife, and also a nickname for a pickpocket.
Shares an ancient root with Latin piscis, as in [[Pisces]]; Old English fisc; similar words appear across Indo-European languages, though biologically there's arguably no such thing as a fish.
Shares an Indo-European ancestor with Latin [[piscis]]; it once meant any sea creature, and its Old English and Middle English plural was fishes.
The Old English plural was fishes; using the singular form as the plural is a Middle English invention.
A German military acronym for an anti-aircraft cannon. In WWII it extended to shells bursting around aircrews, and now means any criticism.
A Crayola colour that began as Flesh Tint (1903), was shortened to Flesh in 1949, was briefly Pink Beige, and became Peach in 1962.
An old word for a butcher, used before English took [[butcher]] from French.
The other French word for river besides [[rivière]]; linked to Latin flumen, the word for the flowing water itself.

term: flies don't enter a closed mouth
original: en boca cerrada no entran moscas
translation: flies don't enter a closed mouth

mentions.note: Advice to keep your mouth shut to stay out of trouble.
An old word for a [[bat]] that the hosts prefer to [[chauve-souris]].
An old imitative word describing the sounds and actions of fighting, like [[hubble-shubble]].
Named because it was played on foot rather than on horseback, unlike 1700s gentlemen's sports, not because of kicking.
Began as before [[noon]], became a word for the morning, and has now largely fallen out of use.
From Latin forestis silva, 'outside woods': royal hunting grounds, not necessarily wooded; related to [[foreign]] and [[sylvan]], and contrasted with Germanic [[wood]].
A unit of two weeks, from Old English for fourteen nights; common in Britain but rarely used in the US; its counterpart was [[sennight]].
Means hardly anyone showed up, roughly like 'one man and his dog'.
A small boiled sausage invented in Frankfurt that became so popular in Vienna that it got called a [[wiener]]; in Frankfurt, it's called a Vienna sausage.
One of several nautical words English got from Dutch.
Jess suggests Freya's day, but Rob says it is generally thought to be Frigg's day; the two goddesses are similar but not identical.
German and Dutch have words like Frosch and vors; Old English had frosc but switched to a form like frogga, perhaps to be cute, like [[dog]].
Like [[dog]], probably began as a cute diminutive and replaced the older word frosh, which German speakers will recognise.
1800s stable slang for horses fed on beans before a race or hunt and in fit condition; it once also meant arrogant or purse-proud.
Originally described a well-fed horse, energetic from its beans and more likely to win a race; nothing to do with feeding people beans.
Spiral pasta whose name means little spindles; discussed in an earlier episode on aeroplane parts alongside [[fuselage]], French for spindle.
An old word for a liar, which Jess says kind of makes sense; she learned it from the card game League of the Lexicon.
From a French word meaning to make merry and eat a lot; it was also the name of a hash.
An old word for a spider, like a little walking weaver, since [[gang]] was an old way of saying walk.
Meant spear in Old English, matching the fish's long spear-like nose; the same gar appears in Beowulf's first line, in Spear-Danes.
A sentence you must reread once you reach the end, because it led you up the garden path, as in 'the horse raced past the barn fell'.
Named after the lizard's noisy call, probably through a Malay or Javanese imitation of the sound.
One of four English borrowings of French [[gentil]], 'nice'; the others are [[gentle]], [[gentile]] and [[jaunty]].
One of four English borrowings of French [[gentil]], 'nice'; the others are [[gentle]], [[genteel]] and [[jaunty]].
One of four English borrowings of French [[gentil]], 'nice'; the others are [[genteel]], [[gentile]] and [[jaunty]].
Literally a description of the earth: geo- means earth, and -graphy means writing, recording or drawing.
A genuine diminutive, from Latin gerbillus, 'little jerboa'; ultimately from a Berber word, also found in Arabic, meaning 'flesh of the loins'.
A brief Middle English name for the [[giraffe]] whose ending was influenced by [[elephant]], a typical ending stuck onto exotic animals.
Named not after Germany but after the English-American chocolate maker Samuel German, whose dark baking chocolate was used in the cake.
What English speakers called the [[hamster]] before the word 'hamster' was adopted.
A white preparatory coating, borrowed from Italian for chalk or plaster, from Latin [[gypsum]] and ultimately Greek; it was traditionally made from rabbit-skin glue and chalk.
Shakespeare is the first recorded written user of 'to ghost' as a verb, which seems surprisingly modern.
Melville's name for the white shark, alongside [[sea attorney]] for brown sharks.
Comes from Arabic zarafa; Middle English also had other names like [[gerfaunt]] and [[orafle]].
Literally a glob; it only came to mean planet Earth around the mid-1500s, not long before the Globe Theatre was named.
Means knuckles; made with potatoes, semolina or wheat flour, and hard to pronounce from its spelling, which Jess used to read as 'noki'.
Dates to at least the early 1900s and was adapted into [[go bananas]].
Adapted from [[go ape]] by linking monkeys with bananas, with 'bananas' alone recorded from the 1920s, though wild monkeys rarely eat bananas.
From Air Force slang, picturing a loop-the-loop going wrong.
Describes someone who trails around after someone else, the way poop dangles behind a goldfish.
Originally called BackRub, because the system checked backlinks to estimate a site's importance.

Named after Sylvester Graham, a Presbyterian minister and dietary reformer whose followers, the Grahamites, made coarse graham flour, bread and crackers; Britons and Americans pronounce Graham differently.
Grand ('big') plus the root meaning 'to talk', so literally 'big talking'; William Barnes proposed [[high-talking]] in its place.
Also called the Platonic year: the roughly 25,920 (now 25,800) years it takes Earth's tilting axis to return to its original position. The hosts don't know Plato's connection.
Named by Erik the Red to attract others to settle there, even though it is clearly not green.
An old verb meaning to displease someone.
Literally means [[pomegranate]], which grenades resemble, and when they explode bits burst out like pomegranate seeds.
A genre name given by people who disliked the music and then adopted by it, like [[punk]].
Actually does come from Guinea, unlike the [[guinea pig]]; guinea fowls were originally called [[turkey|turkeys]].
Neither from Guinea nor a pig: maybe named for pig-like shape and noises, or the guinea hog, with Guinea meaning any far-off land or slave-ship cargo.
A Louisiana stew named after an African word for okra, possibly Bantu, from an unknown language; the dish mixes West African, French, Spanish, German and Choctaw influences.
Originally just a person's name, now used for any person, another example of everyman names.
Gibberish chosen by Reuben and Rose Mattus in the Bronx to sound foreign, vaguely Danish; it doesn't actually mean anything.
The had- part is unknown; -ock is the diminutive suffix of [[buttock]], [[bullock]] and [[hillock]], so a had was bigger than a haddock.
The deepest (hadal) zone, named from the same root as [[Hades]], the underworld.

term: hair of the dog that bit you

mentions.note: Its earliest 16th-century uses mean drinking alcohol for a hangover, not treating dog bites, so the dog-bite cure was probably figurative from the start.
In German (and other Germanic languages) half one means 12:30, halfway to one, whereas in British English it means 1:30, which causes missed meetings.
Literally a steak from Hamburg, formed with the German place suffix [[-er]].
The same name as [[Seamus]], in the vocative form used to address him. English speakers overheard it and took it for a separate name.
From Old High German hamustro, from Russian, ultimately Iranian: Avestan hamaestar means 'one who tramples down', probably because they destroyed crops and food stores.
Means hoarding, buying more than you need like a [[hamster]] storing food in its cheeks; German also has a verb meaning to hoard, and the term surged during the pandemic.
German for a mobile phone. It borrows an English word that doesn't exist in this sense; the German for hand is simply Hand.
The Old Norse word for shark, related to Dutch [[haai]] and German [[Hai]]; Old English lacked a general word for sharks.
From Old English heorot, a word for deer; Heorot is also the hall in Beowulf, named for stags because they were linked with royalty.
The earlier English name for the season now called [[fall]] or [[autumn]]; many other Germanic languages still use their version of harvest.
One of several old words for a liar whose logic Jess doesn't fully understand yet.
From Arabic for 'the die' via French. It named a dice game before meaning risk, and pronouncing the h is an overcorrection.

term: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket
translation: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket

mentions.note: Describes a stingy person: reaching into a pocket with a hedgehog in it would hurt, so they avoid paying.
A [[knobbly monster]] used for Darth Vader.
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.
Possibly a diminutive of a word meaning army, from their schooling; the -ing suffix means associated with, as in [[Viking]].
Means to winterize yourself, and it evokes the French word for winter, [[hiver]].
According to Egyptologist Ilona Regulski, the signs should be called hieroglyphs, not hieroglyphics.
William Barnes's Germanic replacement for [[grandiloquent]].
The Germanic counterpart of Romance [[mountain]]; no fixed height separates the two, and the threshold varies by country and surrounding terrain.
Industry term for bluegrass-style music marketed to white audiences, the counterpart of [[race records]]; it developed into country music.
Another name for the seahorse, literally horse sea monster; also the seahorse-shaped part of the brain.
Means river horse; the potamus part meaning river also appears in [[Mesopotamia]].

term: hoddy-doddy, all arse and no body

mentions.note: Francis Grose's 18th-century Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue records it as London slang for a clumsy person.
Borrowed from French; it was originally the name of a spiced goose stew.
Another unexplained -og word like [[dog]]; similar Celtic words exist, but Old English hog meant males of almost any farm animal, complicating that origin.
The collective noun for hamsters, 'horde' meaning an army rather than hoarding, which fits [[hamster]]'s 'trampler' meaning.
An old word for a timepiece, sundial or hourglass; Rob compares it with the French word for a clock, and it is related to [[horologer]].
A 14th-century word for a clockmaker, from the same source as [[hour]].
Latin word for a timepiece, the source of [[horology]]; we still describe timepieces as horological.
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.
'Playing hot cockles' is a historical term for sex.
Other Germanic languages use a word like hound for dog; it shares a PIE root with [[canine]] and, via Greek, with [[cynic]].
Once the generic word for dogs; it swapped places with [[dog]] and became the more specific, breed-focused term.
From Greek hora, a unit or interval; the H was never pronounced in English, French or Spanish, though it is in [[horology]]. It shares an ancient root with [[year]].
An old word for a builder, one of many [[wright]] job titles.

term: how do you like them apples

mentions.note: Found in 1895 in Texas's Bryan Daily Eagle, boasting about cotton receipts; the WWI toffee-apple mortar story is too late to be the source.
The Old English name for March, which Jess says meant a quick month, or a month of nimbleness and activity.
The Old Norse name for Orkney's Mainland (also called Pomona), with the same horse element as in [[Odobenus rosmarus|rosmarus]].
An old imitative word for a fight or uproar, like [[bobbery]] and [[foofaraw]], from the same family as hullabaloo and kerfuffle.
A 19th-century phrase, probably a pun on [[umbles|umble pie]], a lowly dish of deer entrails given to servants.
A self-explanatory name, referring to the big bumpy part of its back.

translation: triggerfish with a snout like a pig

mentions.note: The Hawaiian name of the reef [[triggerfish]]; its repeated syllables reflect how Hawaiian doubles words to intensify them.
Sir John Cheke's native replacement for centurion in his Gospel of Matthew, written to avoid excessive borrowings in the [[inkhorn]] spirit.
Means hunger makes food taste better; Jess feels it carries historical baggage but is meant optimistically.
Fried cornmeal balls, and to Rob a brand of shoe; the popular story says hunters fed them to dogs to keep them quiet, but the real origin is unknown.
Named by Flóki Vilgerðarson to scare people off, because he thought it a terrible place to settle.
Freud wrote in German and called it das Es, 'the it'; the Latin term id is not his.
A Taylor Swift lyric that became a meme; Jess picked it up without realising it came from the song.
Im- 'not', per 'through' and [[via]] 'road': something with no way through, and so resistant to attack.
Named by detractors; 'impressionists' appears in Louis Leroy's scathing 1874 review, and the name is thought to come from Monet's painting Impression, soleil levant.
Unable to contain yourself, related to [[continent]]; it first meant unrestrained sexual desire and only later referred to the bowels.
Jokingly said by Jess's Indian friends to mean showing up an hour late, like [[Filipino time]].
One of several Italian pasta suffixes, along with -elli, -illi, -etti, -ine and -elle, that mean something small; the opposite of [[-oni]].
Name of the backlash against classical borrowings during the Renaissance; perhaps because long Latinate words meant dipping your quill into an inkhorn again and again.
From Latin for cut into, meaning segmented; the Romans translated the Greek word behind [[entomology]], like calling them cut-ups.
An 18th-century non-hybrid alternative to [[interplanetary]], with mundane meaning worldly.
A hybrid of Latin inter and Greek planet; avoiding such hybrids produced [[intermundane]].
The Italian equivalent of [[break a leg]], which has a set reply, [[may the wolf die]].
Animals without vertebrae, from vertebra meaning joint, referring to the joints of the spine; hence they're spineless.
Related to [[envoy]]: a request for payment to be sent along. There's no voice in it, but there is a road ([[via]]).
Its silent s is only there to match the silent s in [[island]], and it in turn lent the s to [[aisle]].
Cited as sharing the foot element of [[octopus]] yet pluralized the English way, as isopods.
A town in southern France, Rob's wife's hometown, thought to be named after the [[oyster|oysters]] found off its coast.
Rob's wife once said it in English; heavy rain looks like dangling strings, a French equivalent of [[raining cats and dogs]].
From Latin iactare, 'to throw', meaning to swagger, boast or thrash in your sleep; it sounds naughtier than it is, like [[ejaculate]].
From Guarani and Tupi, where the full word means true carnivore: the final part means true, and the rest is their general word for carnivore.
Probably from the Provençal dish jambonetta, maybe linked to French [[jambe]] 'leg' or to giblets, and also to a French word for a mishmash; in 19th-century French it meant a raffle.
[[Hamish]] and [[Seamus]] are both forms of James, which is itself also [[Jacob]].
Late-19th-century American slang for coffee, a blend of [[java]] and [[mocha]], and the likely source of [[cup of joe]].
In Latin a doorkeeper or porter, related to [[Janus]], the two-faced god of doorways; it later meant a school usher, then a caretaker by the 1700s.
Named after [[Janus]], the god related to [[janitor]].
Rob's favourite of the four English borrowings of French [[gentil]], 'nice', alongside [[gentle]], [[genteel]] and [[gentile]].
Fairly modern US slang for someone who talks too much, quoted from the Philadelphia Saturday Evening Post in 1910.
Another fish that isn't a fish, from the old broad use of [[fish]].
Its Jerusalem is just Italian girasole, 'sunflower', and it isn't really an [[artichoke]].
First recorded with this spelling in Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice, modelled on a similar Hebrew name of a minor biblical figure.
A greeting that is bonjour reversed in [[verlan]].
The word diurnal squeezed through French; a doublet of [[diary]].
African-American term for an informal venue with music, dancing and gambling; juke probably comes from a Gullah word meaning rowdy or disorderly.
Named after the [[juke joint]].
Juke is from a Wolof and Gullah word for rowdy. Coin-operated jukeboxes were named after [[juke joint|juke joints]], where Black people in the southeastern US danced, drank and gambled.
From Hindi for any wilderness or uncultivated land, from a Sanskrit word for arid terrain; English speakers applied it to dense forest.
Means what you deserve; almost an eggcorn, since people assume it refers to [[dessert]], though both come from the same verb meaning to serve.
The first day of the Roman month, from [[calare]] meaning to call out, because priests publicly proclaimed it after observing the new moon.
A popular myth says it comes from a phrase meaning 'I don't know', said when someone asked what the animal was.
The Greek word for shark, literally jagged biter.
German word for a male cat that also means a hangover; the hosts don't know why, which leads them to [[hair of the dog that bit you]].

links.target: hair of the dog that bit you

mentions.note: Short for katsuretsu, the Japanese version of English [[cutlet]] adapted to Japanese sound rules, which English then borrowed back as a [[boomerang word]].

translation: to become, to happen, to develop, to create

mentions.note: A triliteral verb written with the scarab sign, because the Egyptian word for scarab had the same three consonants.
They were said to be originally called whale killers because they hunt baleen whales; the hosts debate whether it is really a whale or a dolphin.
A Sino-Korean word that has changed over time; the word it comes from literally means submerged vegetables.
A [[kimchi]] soup; jjigae just means soup.
Not a garden where children play but a figurative garden where children grow like sweet little flowers.
Another collective noun found in the Book of St Albans alongside [[litter of whelps]].
Its -dom is unrelated to dominion but related to [[doom]]: Old English dom meant a law or judgment, so a kingdom is a territory defined by decree.
Probably a variation on French chaton, 'little cat', from chat.
The English word, as in having the knack of something, which can also mean a snap, comes from the same Germanic root as [[knackwurst]].
A parboiled sausage named after German knacken 'to crackle', because it bursts; Americans often say 'knockwurst', which Rob calls wrong; it shares a Germanic root with [[knack]].
An overly elaborate synonym journalists use to avoid repeating a word; the name itself is one such way of referring to a crocodile.
American, first recorded in 1891, so not from OED editor C. T. Onions; the Cockney rhyming slang onion rings = things is possible but puzzling.
Means power station, chosen because the band was into industry.
Simply a Norwegian word for tiny shrimp, one of many fishing words borrowed through contact between Norwegian and English sailors.

German for art; künstlich ('artificial') comes from it, just as English [[artificial]] comes from [[art]], so AI is künstliche Intelligenz (KI) in German.
A gymnasium near Athens where Antisthenes taught, possibly the source of the name [[cynic]].
The Italian name of the [[Mona Lisa]], meaning 'the happy one' and punning on the sitter's name, Lisa del Giocondo.
A short-lived English word meaning muscular, literally lizardy, for the same reason as [[muscle]].
Title of an album by Renaud; it looks like "leave concrete" but is [[verlan]] for laisse tomber, meaning let it go or just leave it.
From Latin lacus, 'basin' or 'reservoir': named for the space that holds the water, not the water itself.

Means tossed noodles; like [[chow mein]], its name contains the word for noodles.

Lory, a Malay bird name, plus -keet from [[parakeet]], a [[cranberry morpheme]] from an Italian diminutive element.
The Macarena singers; the name means those from the river.
The band behind La Bamba; the name means the wolves.
Deliberately misspelled but still pronounced Leonard Skinner, after a gym teacher at the band's school.

Literally 'to hold in the hand', from [[tenere]]; an example of how literal Latin compounds really are.
Justin Bieber's capuchin monkey, named after the rapper Mally Mall, who gave it to him.
Animals with mammary glands that suckle their young; related to [[mama]] and, Rob notes, to the place name [[Manchester]].

The Italian Eurovision-winning band has a Danish name meaning moonlight, suggested by their half-Danish bassist.
Latin for 'hand', whose plural is also manus, not mani.
An Old English word for a wetland.

The reply to [[into the wolf's mouth]]; the hosts wonder whether the wolf chokes on you or dies before it can swallow.

translation: mention a wolf and the wolf is there

mentions.note: A listener-submitted Lithuanian equivalent of [[speak of the devil]].

The name of the middle layer of the ocean, built on the same pelagic element as [[epipelagic]].

The heartland of cuneiform, literally the area between two rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris.
Decorative dots that bands like Mötley Crüe, Motörhead and Spinal Tap put on letters to look Germanic and dark.

translation: a thing high up in the air

Young French people's word for a woman, from femme with its sounds reversed in [[verlan]].
A small [[biome]], such as the gut bacteria Rob thought of first.

Typically a surname before Shakespeare used it in The Tempest.
An Old Norse word for a marsh.
From an Ojibwe term meaning great river, so 'Mississippi River' is 'great river river'.
A northern English dialect word meaning to bother someone, which Rob says is a relative of [[bemoidered]].
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.

From a passage in Virginia Woolf's story The Mark on the Wall mentioning "modest mouse-coloured people."
A French word for something soft and oozing, like a chocolate cake; related to [[mollusk]].
From Latin mollis, soft, originally the gooey ones before shelled species were included; related to French [[moelleux]] and English [[melt]].
A medieval unit of time: a tenth of a [[point]], made up of twelve [[ounce|ounces]].
An old word for a scarecrow from Coleridge's dictionary, which reminds Rob of [[emmet]].
Mona is a contraction of [[Madonna]], 'my lady'; this is only the English name, since in Italian the painting is called [[La Gioconda]].
Moon day; the moon is named in both Monday and every [[month]].
Most likely [[back slang]] for [[nickname]], which reversed comes out close to moniker, though moniker oddly sounds more formal.
An old word for either a rhinoceros or a unicorn, meaning anything with a single horn; Rob found it in Herbert Coleridge's dictionary.
A [[knobbly monster]] journalists used to avoid repeating the word badger.

Basically means a measurement, related to [[meter]], [[dimension]], [[menstrual]], [[menopause]], [[semester]] and [[trimester]]; it roughly matches a lunar cycle, so the moon names it.
French word for a [[watch]], meaning show, because the device shows the time.
Bigger than the [[elk]] and a different animal, though moose are called elk in some parts of the world.
A unit of a word, a bit like a syllable but not quite.
Something that rises above the earth; related to [[mount]], [[mound]], [[eminent]], [[menace]], [[promontory]] and [[prominent]], which all share a sense of sticking out.
A fit of the blues, or sometimes a vague abdominal pain; its exact origin is unknown.
From Arabic mumia, an embalmed body; in English it first meant a medicinal substance made from bitumen or Egyptian corpses, which people ate for centuries.
Someone who stubbornly insists they're right; spread by Erasmus's story of a priest who kept saying 'mumpsimus' instead of 'sumpsimus' in 'quod ore sumpsimus'.

The same word as [[mussel]], meaning little mouse; a rippling muscle supposedly looks like a mouse crawling under the skin.
Another sea mouse: the same word as [[muscle]], spelled differently, both meaning little mouse, perhaps because mussels resemble little mice stuck to things.
From Spanish mestengo, 'stray animal'. That comes from the Mesta, a livestock owners' council said to mean 'mixed', perhaps for dividing mixed strays; not mixed breeds.

Originally an insult for humans meaning mutton-head, then for dogs (perhaps dim or scolded for sheep worrying), and now insults humans again.
The German word for placenta; Rob notes German medical terms are often literal, whereas English euphemizes through Greek and Latin.
The French counterpart of [[a little bird told me]], said while holding up the finger; its origin is harder to work out.

The division of [[Cetacea]] made up of the baleen whales, such as humpbacks.
Short for the National Biscuit Company, which made the [[graham cracker]] what it is today and released the Mallomar in 1913.
Named after Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya, who made the dish up in 1943 at the Victory Club across the border from Texas and called it Nacho's special.
Named after maître d' Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya, who improvised them in 1943 at Mexico's Victory Club for US officers' wives.
Probably corpse whale, from its mottled grey look under the surface; an alternative links it to knal, needle, because of its tusk.
Means sailor; early bestiaries described it floating with arms spread like sails, perhaps an image from the [[argonaut]]; the ship is probably named after it.
Said before a hunt to wish that you catch neither mammal nor bird; the expected reply is 'go to hell'.
From German Kupfernickel, 'copper goblin' or 'copper devil'. Miners gave it that name because the copper-coloured ore yielded no copper, and Nickel was a nickname for the devil.
From 'an ekename', which became 'a nickname'; reversed in [[back slang]], it probably gave [[moniker]].
Means to grip or press with the hands, as the chef does to shape the rice under the fish, so it looks pressed in a palm.
Sanskrit for blowing away or wiping out; in Buddhism it means release from karma and rebirth, having blown away life's entanglements.
The opposite of [[placebo]], as in the nocebo effect. It sounds made up, but it's genuine Latin for 'I will cause harm'.

French for north, borrowed from English [[north]] and passed on to Spanish, even though Latin had its own compass words.
From an ancient root meaning left: if you face the rising sun in the east, north is on your left.

Ob-, here 'in front of or before', plus fuscare, 'to make dark'.

Ob- plus scurus, 'covered', the same element as in [[chiaroscuro]].

From the Latin for west, the counterpart of [[orient]].

French for west, borrowed from English [[west]], like the other French compass points, and then into Spanish.

Latin for 'I will please', from the opening of a prayer and later applied to drugs; its opposite is [[nocebo]].

Something that occurs earlier on your route or path, from [[via]].

Thomas Harman's 1500s term for a horse thief.

Thought to come from French poupée 'doll', the same word that gives [[puppet]] and [[poppet]].
Comes from porphyra, a valuable pigment that was traded as a symbol of wealth.
An imitative sound used to call a cat, like [[meow]].
From Greek pyramis, which is probably Egyptian and also meant a pyramid-shaped honey cake; every pyramid, even in the Americas, is named after the Egyptian ones.
The word for something pear-shaped, which Rob looked up while discussing [[go pear-shaped]].
The more advanced studies that followed the [[trivium]]: arithmetic, astronomy, music and geometry.
Despite sounding heroic, it meant someone who habitually made money from spurious lawsuits, something like an ambulance chaser.
The signature on Duchamp's Fountain; Rob reads it as a pun on German Armut, 'poverty'.
Music-industry term used from the 1920s to the 1940s for records marketed to African-American audiences.
A modern term from early-1900s ecology that became the preferred scientific name for the biome, contrasted with [[jungle]].
Covered in an earlier episode; the idea may be that rain washed cats and dogs living in roofs out into the street.
A Greek equivalent of [[raining cats and dogs]].

mentions.note: One of the idioms Rob's wife Elodie recommended; another French equivalent of [[raining cats and dogs]].

mentions.note: Jess reads it as bad parenting choices coming back to haunt you, or more generally like 'you reap what you sow'.
A Japanese version of a Chinese name meaning pulled noodles; the 'men' at the end means noodles, as in [[chow mein]].
Named after their own song about the air-show crash at the US base Ramstein; the extra M comes from a misspelling on their equipment.
Jess's long-legged dog, named in homage to Aragorn, the ranger nicknamed Longshanks in The Lord of the Rings.
A crude word from Francis Grose's 1785 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue for a man whose scrotum hangs longer than his penis.
A Grose word, supposedly related to [[rantallion]], for a sexual position with the woman on top facing the opposite direction.

Origin unknown; theories include 'little turnips', though turnips were never part of it, and a word for a robe, though early ravioli could be unwrapped meatballs.
Spelling a word with pictures of things that sound like its parts, as some hieroglyphs do; for example, a bee plus a leaf for 'belief'.
We call him by his first name; his surname van Rijn means 'of the river Rhine', and Harmenszoon is a patronymic meaning 'son of Harmen'.
From a Latin word meaning crawling, describing animals that are low to the ground.
The French word for shark, whose meaning Jess finds scary; the explanation is garbled in the transcript.
The Spanish [[spill the beans]]; the hosts aren't sure what the secret cake refers to.
Reportedly coined by Billboard magazine as a euphemism to replace [[race records|race music]] for music of Black origin.
Relates to rivers and streams, but in Latin originally to riverbanks; related to [[river]].
The Left Bank of the Seine in Paris; rive comes from the same Latin word as [[river]].
From Latin riparia, 'riverbank', while flumen and amnis named the water itself, so a river is named for its bank; see [[riparian]].
French for river, from the same Latin root as [[river]]; the hosts can't say how it differs from [[fleuve]], guessing one is bigger.
Originally a diminutive of Robert, just as [[parrot]] comes from Pierrot, a cute form of Peter.
First used of ships at sea, then as African-American slang and a sexual euphemism; the OED prefers rock 'n' roll, and DJ Alan Freed popularised the genre label.
From an Italian word for a bobbin or small distaff used in spinning; it applies to both space and firework rockets.
A lighter, playful late form of [[Baroque]]; it means shell work or rock work, from French rocaille with a playful repeated sound, so the word is partly made up.
Borrowed from Old French, from a late Latin sense of 'in the Roman manner'; it gave Romance languages and romances for novels that celebrated the classics.
Named after Rosetta, the French name for Rashid, where Napoleon's soldiers found it in 1799; its Greek, Demotic and hieroglyphic text helped decipher hieroglyphs.
A dog that roves and adventures; popularised by the 1905 British film Rescued by Rover, and similar in meaning to [[Ranger]].
Duchamp's female alter ego, a pun on the French phrase 'Éros, c'est la vie', 'sex is life'.
In Thomas Harman's 1500s rogue literature, a former soldier who harasses people.
Means desert, so 'Sahara Desert' is literally 'desert desert', a [[pleonasm]].
The only country named after a real historical woman, St Lucy of Syracuse; French sailors named it after arriving on her feast day.
Taken from French, where it meant lettuce, and further back from the Roman sense of salted; Rob notes that in Germany it covers anything heavy with mayonnaise.
From Cleopatra's line in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra: being green and cold like lettuce means naive, like unripe fruit.
Probably Persian, meaning 'inside flame', from the myth that salamanders were born in fire because they crawled from burning rotten logs; heraldic ones look dragon-like.
Said to be an ancient Sumerian word meaning plunge earth, as Bedouin hunters launched the dogs off camels' backs for a running start.
Said to be an ancient Sumerian word meaning 'plunge earth', supposedly because the dogs leapt off camels' backs during hunts.
It shares its flesh element with [[sarcophagus]]: being sarcastic is tearing at someone's flesh.
A fish whose name uses sarcastic in its root sense of flesh-tearing, as in [[sarcasm]], for its large mouth with scary teeth.

Fresh fish served on its own, without the rice that makes a dish [[sushi]].
Named for Saturn, a return to Latin among the otherwise Germanic day names.
An old word for Friday evening, the eve of Saturday.
The lizard-hipped dinosaurs; they, not the bird-hipped [[ornithischian|ornithischians]], are the ones that became birds.
From Spanish sabana, 'treeless plain', from Taíno zabana: a Caribbean word that Europeans later applied to the African biome.
Taken from the end of [[landscape]] and reused in words like seascape and hellscape; the hosts discuss whether this counts as [[rebracketing]].
German for growler.

A school of fish is borrowed from Middle Dutch and related to [[shoal]]. It is unrelated to the educational school, whose basic sense is leisure.
German for sponge or mushroom, related to [[swamp]]; TV make-up artists used a Schwämmchen, a little sponge, on Rob.
A Middle English harvest party, one of several -ale party words like the bride-ale behind [[bridal]].

Named because a land [[urchin]] was a hedgehog, just as Greek echinos meant both hedgehog and sea urchin.
Essentially means a sowing; it was used more generally until the 14th century, when four fixed seasons were settled on.
Same word as ordinal second, from Latin [[secunda minuta]], a second reduction of the hour. Before the Normans brought it, English used [[other]] instead.
Doing something of your own accord without any real cause; it made Rob snort and blush.
The French [[spill the beans]], picturing a mine whose fuse was accidentally left sticking out, showing where the bomb is.
From Latin for six months, not half a year's worth of months; related to [[month]] and [[trimester]], though semesters no longer last six months.
From Old English for seven nights, a unit of seven days and counterpart of [[fortnight]]; no longer used.
The genus name of cuttlefish, and also the brown pigment once made from their ink.
Latin for cuttlefish. In English it came to name the brown pigment once made from [[cuttlefish]] ink, hence sepia photo filters.
The classical Latin for north, meaning 'seven ploughs': Ursa Major, called the Plough or Big Dipper, which points to the North Star.
From the Maa language of the Maasai, meaning endless plain.
A woman who sewed for a living, before the French-derived -ess ending gave seamstress; formed with [[-ster]].
A historical term for sex, recorded centuries ago.
Entered English in the 1400s meaning scoundrel, villain or swindler, naming the fish only from the 1700s; origin uncertain, probably Germanic.

Not a fish; the name reflects the older meaning of [[fish]] as any sea-dwelling animal.
Egyptian name for the Sphinx statue, which Susan Wise Bauer proposes as the source of Greek [[Sphinx]]; most sources disagree.
A Japanese breed name, perhaps after the brushwood landscape where it hunted or its golden coat.
Usually translated as little brushwood dog, referring to either their fur color or the landscape they were bred to hunt in.
From Chinese, literally lion dog, another word hiding a lion.
A suffix as in lordship and friendship, also found in [[landscape]]; it is related to [[shape]], means shaped like, and German has -schaft.

In the same family as [[shirt]] and [[skirt]], which both mean a short garment.
From Latin scrinium, a chest; it came to mean a chest holding a saint's relic, then a venerated place itself.

Irish and Scottish Gaelic for westward, also meaning behind you, because people oriented themselves facing the sunrise.
Means victory rose; it's also the name of the lead singer's younger sister, born as the band formed, written as one word.
Named after Étienne de Silhouette, a frugal French controller-general of the 1750s; the reason is unclear: cheapness, his short term in office, or his own silhouette-making.
Mentioned as the Latin for left-handed, the counterpart to the right-handedness in [[ambidextrous]].
Word in the local Treviso dialect for a brothel madam, used in the tiramisu academy's aphrodisiac origin story for [[tiramisu]].
From Dutch schets, from Italian schizzo, and ultimately from Greek schedios, meaning temporary or made offhand, via an unattested Latin word.
One of several nautical words English got from Dutch.
The Old Norse version of Old English [[shirt]]; both mean a short garment, like [[shorts]].
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.

[[back slang]] for police.

One of several nautical words English got from Dutch.

A cute Norwegian expression for heavy snowfall.
Short for association football; a British English term.

Sleepwalking; the word Rob was reaching for after [[obambulation]].

From French sorcier, so Rob argues it should really just be 'sorcer'; Jess says English is working too hard.

Badly done [[spaghetti]] left in the water too long, formed with the suffix [[-acci]].

First used in 1993, when Richard Depew accidentally posted one message 200 times to Usenet. It references the Monty Python sketch of Vikings singing 'spam'.

Short for 'speak of the devil and he will appear'; many languages have variants.
Named because the waxy [[spermaceti]] in its head, used for focusing sound and buoyancy, looks like sperm.

From a Greek word meaning 'squeeze, bind, embrace', after the riddling Greek Sphinx. Susan Wise Bauer suggests it may instead corrupt Egyptian [[shesep ankh]].

To reveal gossip on purpose, unlike the accidental [[spill the beans]]; it comes from late-20th-century Black drag culture, where 'T' meant truth, and Lady Chablis used it in 1994.
One of Rob's favourite old names for a spider, essentially 'web spinner' with a fancy verb form.

Rob says Dick, like Jack and Joe, was a popular everyman name, which is why we have things like spotted dick.
Thought to be a sailors' variant of [[squirt]], referring to its inking; a group is a shoal, though some advocate calling it a squad.
Origin unknown; possibly a sailors' variant of [[squirt]], since squid squirt.
From French, originally Greek, meaning 'shadow tail' and possibly related to [[obscure]]; supposedly the longest one-syllable word in English.
British name for what Americans call whipped cream; in Britain, whipped cream means liquid cream that has been whipped by hand.
Another odd -g word like [[dog]]; originally a male deer in its fifth year, with related words elsewhere meaning males of various species.

William Barnes's Germanic alternative to astronomy.

Named after a dildo in William S. Burroughs's Naked Lunch, because the band loved Beat Generation literature.

Greek for a standing block or slab; the Rosetta Stone is a broken piece of one.

A slightly newer version of [[tempest in a teapot]], with the same idea.

A sign that stands for a syllable, which later cuneiform adopted.

From Attabi, a striped silk cloth made in Baghdad's Attabi district; once imported to England, its wavy striped pattern gave the cat its name.

Close to [[pleonasm]] but also used in maths; tautologies like 'ATM machine' sound more obviously repetitive.

Caravaggio's dramatic lighting, in which figures emerge from a deep, dark background.
Latin 'to hold', found in [[maintain]], abstain, entertain, obtain and detain.

The order that includes all [[turtle|turtles]], tortoises and terrapins, from Latin testa 'shell'.
A pun on beetles and beat, partly inspired by Buddy Holly's Crickets; coined by John Lennon and Stuart Sutcliffe.

Light that comes between, when the sun is below the horizon; originally it referred to both morning and evening, not just the end of the day.
